candidate.blueprint_locator: Printed page 14, Physiological Adaptation: manage care of a client receiving hemodialysis; recognize client complications and intervene.
candidate.educational_objective: Teach daily AV-fistula surveillance for infection findings and the expected blood-flow vibration, with prompt reporting if the vibration is lost.

options.A: I will check the access every day for redness or warmth and make sure I can still feel the usual vibration.
options.B: I only need to check the access on days when I receive dialysis.
options.C: If I cannot feel the usual vibration after dialysis, I can wait until the next scheduled treatment to report it.
options.D: Redness and warmth over the access are expected unless I also develop a fever.

candidate.rationale: NIDDK instructs clients to protect the hemodialysis access, wash the area daily, check for warmth or redness, and confirm the vibration produced by blood flow; the dialysis center should be notified if the vibration cannot be felt. A reflects correct surveillance. B omits daily monitoring, C delays reporting possible loss of flow, and D incorrectly normalizes local infection findings.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Daily AV-access care includes checking for infection and the expected blood-flow vibration and reporting loss of that vibration.
candidate.source_locator: Take care of your access: wash area daily; check warmth/redness; a working access has a palpable vibration; notify the dialysis center if the vibration cannot be felt. Possible problems: access infection or poor blood flow/blockage.
candidate.source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
candidate.stem: A client with a hemodialysis arteriovenous fistula is reviewing home access care. Which statement shows correct understanding?
